title: Git
summary: History, branches and how to recover from mistakes.
why: AI assistants will happily rewrite your history. Knowing what a rebase or a reset really does is what lets you review, undo and trust those changes.

cards.question: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
cards.answer: fetch downloads remote changes without touching your branch or working directory. pull is fetch followed by merge (or rebase, if configured).

cards.question: What is the staging area for?
cards.answer: It lets you choose exactly which changes go into the next commit, even parts of a file with git add -p, to build small, coherent commits.

cards.question: Merge or rebase? When to use each?
cards.answer: merge joins two histories with a merge commit and preserves the real history. rebase replays your commits on a new base and gives a linear history, but rewrites hashes. Rule: never rebase branches others have already pulled.

cards.question: What is the difference between git reset and git revert?
cards.answer: reset moves the branch pointer and rewrites history (--soft keeps index and files, --mixed keeps the working directory, --hard discards everything). revert creates a new commit that undoes another, so it is safe on shared branches.

cards.question: You ran reset --hard and lost commits. How do you recover them?
cards.answer: With git reflog, which locally records where HEAD and branches have pointed. Find the previous hash and run git reset --hard or git branch new <hash>. Unreachable commits are kept for about 30 days before cleanup.

cards.question: How do you find which commit introduced a bug?
cards.answer: With git bisect: mark one bad and one good commit and Git binary-searches between them. With git bisect run <script> you automate it if you have a failing test.
